title: Low-energy collective electronic excitations in a gold monolayer
authors: Vyacheslav M. Silkin, Maxim Yu. Kagan
abstract: The low-energy plasmonic properties of a free-standing Au(111) monolayer, frequently referred to as goldene, are investigated by time-dependent density functional theory in the random phase approximation. In the evaluation of dielectric and loss functions the first-principle band structure characterized by a single $s-p$ energy band at the Fermi level is taken into account. In this system with apparently simple band structure around the Fermi surface the calculations show the presence, besides the standard two-dimensional (2D) plasmon mode, at even lower energies of three anomalous branches in the momentum-energy region usually assigned to incoherent electron-hole pairs. This is an unexpected result since the electronic system of the gold monolayer is characterized by a single energy band crossing the Fermi level. The dispersion of these anomalous plasmonic branches is strongly anisotropic in-plane and gapless. A general feature is that at small in-plane momentum transfers the modes have a sound-like dispersion in certain momentum directions. We rely the appearance of these anomalous modes to a notable deviation of the Fermi surface of a gold monolayer from a circular shape. As a result of its almost perfect hexagon shape, there is possibility to realize in a {\it single} electronic energy band a scenario of a multi-component electron system with the carrier groups moving with different Fermi velocities in certain momentum directions. The found modes correspond to the out-of-phase charge oscillations of the carriers at different sides of the hexagonal Fermi surface. Hence our work presents evidence how in a metal system with apparently simple band structure around the Fermi level its shape can result in conversion of single-particle charge excitations into collective charge excitations.
summary: This work uses advanced DFT calculations to study plasmons in a gold monolayer, finding unexpected low-energy collective excitations beyond the standard plasmon mode. These anomalous modes are linked to the hexagonal geometry of the Fermi surface, suggesting the system behaves like a multi-component electron gas despite having a simple single-band electronic structure.
main_problem: The study investigates the low-energy collective electronic excitations (plasmons) in a free-standing Au(111) monolayer.
main_result: The gold monolayer exhibits anomalous, gapless, and anisotropic plasmonic branches at low energies, which are attributed to the hexagonal shape of the Fermi surface allowing for multi-component carrier oscillations.
method: Time-dependent density functional theory (TDDFT) within the random phase approximation (RPA) is employed to calculate the dielectric and loss functions.
model_or_system: The physical system is a free-standing Au(111) monolayer. The electronic structure is characterized by a single s-p energy band crossing the Fermi level, but the Fermi surface exhibits a pronounced hexagonal shape.
key_observables: Plasmon dispersion relations, dielectric function ($\epsilon_M$), and loss functions ($	ext{Im}[\epsilon^{-1}(\mathbf{q}, \omega)]$).
important_parameters: Low in-plane momentum transfers ($\mathbf{q}$), Fermi energy ($E_F$), and doping levels (e.g., 0.17 electron doping).
main_assumptions: The calculations are performed in the RPA, and approximations like using a Gaussian for the $\delta$-function are noted.
figures_summary: Figures show the electronic band structure, 2D energy band dispersion, and the momentum-energy plots of the plasmonic modes, revealing both the standard 2D plasmon and the novel low-energy branches.
paper_structure: The paper systematically calculates the response function using TDDFT/RPA, analyzes the resulting dielectric function along high-symmetry directions ([10] and [01]), and compares the findings to Free-Electron Gas theory to establish the origin of the anomalous modes.
why_interesting: The discovery of low-energy, sound-like plasmons arising from the geometry of a single energy band is a fascinating example of how band structure topology can induce complex collective behavior, relevant to understanding charge dynamics in 2D materials.
